entry.title: Run a Local Model With Ollama

link.title: Run a Local Model With Ollama

entry.content:
Studying LLM Behavior · Model setup

After testing the pipeline with the mock backend, the next step is to connect a real model. Ollama downloads and runs a model on the local computer, then provides an API that the pipeline can call.

The setup below uses a locally downloaded model. Ollama also offers cloud models, so the application name alone no longer establishes where a model ran. When prompts or responses must remain local, cloud features should be disabled and that setting recorded. Ollama describes its cloud models in the cloud documentation and explains how to disable cloud features in its FAQ.

Install Ollama

Ollama provides installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux through its official quickstart. More detailed instructions are available for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

After installation, open a new terminal and run the command below. The Ollama commands used on this page are the same on Windows, macOS, and Linux:

ollama -v

The command should return the installed Ollama version. If the command is not recognized, close and reopen the terminal.

On Windows and macOS, opening the Ollama application normally starts the local service. A Linux installation may run it as a system service. If Ollama was installed manually and is not already running, start it in a separate terminal:

ollama serve

Leave that terminal open during the checks below. By default, the pipeline will reach the service at http://localhost:11434. In this address, localhost means the same computer on which the pipeline is running.

Choose a model the computer can support

For this check, select a model that fits the available computer. This is a setup decision, not a substitute for choosing the model required by the research question. Replacing that model with a smaller one changes the object being studied.

The commands below use the 3-billion-parameter Qwen 2.5 instruction model:

ollama pull qwen2.5:3b

This model is smaller than many commonly used instruction models, but it is not guaranteed to fit or run quickly on every computer. The download also requires several gigabytes of storage. The Ollama model library lists other models and sizes.

Once it finishes, list the locally available models:

ollama ls

Copy the model name exactly as shown by ollama ls. Then retrieve the model information:

curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags

The command returns a list of the models on the computer. The section for this model will include two fields like these:

{
  "name": "qwen2.5:3b",
  "digest": "a long string of letters and numbers"
}

The digest identifies the downloaded Ollama package more precisely than a name such as qwen2.5:3b, which may remain unchanged after the package is updated. Record both values. A broad label such as “Qwen” or “Qwen 2.5” does not identify the model precisely enough.

The Ollama setup and the later vLLM demonstration use models from the same Qwen 2.5 3B family, but they should not be treated as identical deployments. Ollama may use quantized weights or format the chat differently. Record these differences when comparing results across the two setups.

Before connecting the pipeline, ask the model for one response directly:

ollama run qwen2.5:3b "Reply with only the word READY."

The wording may not be exactly READY. At this stage, the command only shows that the model can generate text. It is not an experimental trial.

Downloading and loading are two different steps. ollama pull saves the model files to the computer’s storage. When ollama run is called, Ollama loads that model into the available CPU or GPU memory so that it can generate a response. Ollama usually keeps the model in memory for a period after the response, which allows ollama ps to report how it was loaded.

Confirm how the local model is using the computer

Immediately after the test response, run:

ollama ps

The output reports whether the model is using the CPU, GPU, or both. It also reports the context currently allocated to the model. A model running on the CPU has not necessarily failed, but collecting many responses may take much longer. Ollama explains the processor values in its FAQ.

If the study requires local-only operation, disable Ollama’s cloud features before data collection and preserve that setting with the study documentation. Do not infer that a model ran locally from the application name alone.

Connect the pipeline to Ollama

Return to the terminal where the llm-behavior-pipeline environment is active. From that folder, copy the example model registry. On macOS or Linux, run:

cp model-registry.yaml.example model-registry.yaml

On Windows PowerShell, run:

Copy-Item model-registry.yaml.example model-registry.yaml

Open model-registry.yaml in a text editor and set its Ollama entry to:

ollama-local:
  backend: ollama
  base_url: http://localhost:11434/v1
  served_name: qwen2.5:3b

ollama-local is the name used by the experiment. base_url points to Ollama’s local chat-completions endpoint, and served_name must match the name returned by ollama ls. Ollama documents the /v1 route as part of its OpenAI compatibility API; the phrase describes the request format, not who developed or hosts the model.

The working registry is ignored by Git because other entries may contain private endpoints. Preserve a sanitized copy of this entry with the study record.

Send the first pipeline request to the model

With Ollama running and the pipeline environment active, run:

python smokes/smoke_chat.py --model ollama-local

The output should name ollama-local, contain a generated reply, and include response metadata. Unlike MOCK_RESPONSE, the reply is produced by a generative model and does not need to match an example word for word.

If the connection is refused, check that the Ollama application or ollama serve is still running. If the model is not found, compare served_name with ollama ls, including the text after the colon.

A generated response confirms that the pipeline can reach Ollama and save what it returns. Task understanding is tested later with the behavioral demonstration.

Session length changes the memory required

The pipeline test introduced the growing trajectory: each new trial can include the instructions and earlier turns from the same session. The input therefore becomes longer as the session proceeds, and the longest valid trajectory must fit within the model’s context length.

Ollama’s context defaults depend on the available memory. Increasing the context also increases memory use (Ollama context-length documentation). For a short smoke test, the default is sufficient. Before collecting data, estimate the longest possible trajectory, leave room for the response, and set the context length before freezing the protocol.

A larger context is not automatically better. It can make the study slower or cause a model that fit on the GPU to move partly into system memory. Record the allocated context shown by ollama ps, and do not change it midway through a run without documenting the change.

Preserve the environment used to generate the responses

The local setup still has to be documented. Before collecting data, preserve:

  • the output of ollama -v;
  • the exact model name, identifier, and full digest;
  • the processor allocation and context length from ollama ps;
  • the sanitized registry entry used by the study;
  • the generation settings;
  • the operating system and available CPU, RAM, and GPU memory; and
  • whether Ollama cloud features were enabled or disabled.

Running the model locally removes some provider-side uncertainty, but it does not make the environment self-documenting. The Ollama version, model file, quantization, drivers, and hardware are all part of the conditions under which the responses were produced.

Ask an agent to help with the local setup

After the pipeline passes its offline mock tests, an agent can inspect the computer and help connect Ollama. Installing software and downloading a model change the computer and may use substantial disk space, so the prompt requires approval before either action.

I have downloaded and tested the llm-behavior-pipeline with its mock backend.
I now want to connect it to a model that runs locally through Ollama.

First inspect, without changing anything:

- my operating system, CPU, RAM, GPU and GPU memory, and free disk space;
- whether Ollama is installed and running;
- which Ollama models are already downloaded; and
- the pipeline's model-registry example and smoke test.

Explain what you find in plain language. Recommend a small instruction-tuned
model that is likely to fit, but do not install Ollama or download a model
until I approve the exact action and expected download size. Do not select a
cloud model. If local-only operation is required, verify that Ollama cloud
features are disabled.

After approval, use the official Ollama instructions for my operating system.
Record the Ollama version, exact model name, identifier, digest, processor
split, and allocated context length. Add the model to model-registry.yaml
without changing the experimental task, then run the pipeline smoke test. Do
not run a full experiment or incur paid charges. Report every command used,
any files changed, and the complete smoke-test result.

A successful smoke test confirms that the pipeline can reach the model and save its response. A behavioral experiment must also vary a condition, repeat the procedure, and connect each response to the trial that produced it.

entry.title: First or Second: How LLMs Judge Competing Responses

link.title: First or Second: How LLMs Judge Competing Responses

entry.content:
Studying LLM Behavior · Behavioral demonstration

Language models are increasingly being used to evaluate the responses of other language models. The judge receives a question and two answers, then decides which answer is better. This makes large evaluations easier to run, but it also

answers appeared in the opposite order?

Shi et al. studied this question across several judge models and tasks. They found that reversing the answers could change which one was preferred, and that the size and direction of this position effect varied across models and evaluation settings. The effect was generally larger when the two answers were closer in quality (Shi et al., 2025).

The demonstration adapts the answer-swapping procedure to a small subset of MT-Bench. It retains the published questions, model answers, and central swap, while using fewer items and a different judge model.

This is a pipeline demonstration, not a standalone benchmark study. Its purpose is to show how a published procedure can be constructed, run, and recorded with the infrastructure developed in this series. The small sample and single judge model are not intended as a replication test, an extension study, or an estimate of the prevalence or size of position effects across LLMs.

The answers change position, not identity

For every question, the judge sees the same pair of answers twice. Only their positions change.

Suppose the underlying answers are X and Y. If the judge selects A when X is in position A, then selects B after X moves to position B, the visible letter has changed but the preferred content has not. The choice is content-consistent across positions. If the judge selects A in both orders, it has switched from X to Y and has favored the first position.

The analysis therefore cannot treat A and B as the outcomes. Each letter has to be mapped back to the answer occupying that position.

The swap makes it possible to distinguish three different patterns:

  • Repetition stability: Does the judge choose the same A/B positional option when an identical trial is repeated?
  • Answer-identity consistency across positions: Does the judge continue to prefer the same underlying answer, X or Y, when that answer moves to a different A/B position? Shi et al. call this measure position consistency.
  • Positional preference: When its choice changes, does it tend to favor the first answer or the second?

A judge can be highly stable and still be sensitive to position. It could, for example, consistently choose whichever answer appears first.

What was retained from the published procedure

Zheng et al. introduced MT-Bench to evaluate chatbot responses, including comparisons made by an LLM judge (Zheng et al., 2023). The public FastChat repository contains the questions, judge prompts, evaluation code, and instructions for retrieving pre-generated model answers (MT-Bench repository).

The demonstration uses 12 MT-Bench questions: three each from writing, reasoning, STEM, and humanities. The original MT-Bench archive contains responses generated by several models. For each question, the response recorded for Vicuna is paired separately with the responses recorded for Alpaca, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4, producing 36 pairs. The questions and comparison models were selected before the Qwen responses were examined.

Each pair appears in both orders, with each order repeated three times. The published MT-Bench judge prompt already includes an instruction telling the judge not to allow answer order to influence its decision. That instruction is important here because the experiment is testing whether order nevertheless changes which underlying answer content is preferred.

The published prompt is compared with a second version in which only this warning has been removed.

This type of comparison is called an ablation. One component is removed while the rest of the procedure remains unchanged. Here, the removed component is a single instruction telling the judge not to let answer order influence its decision. Comparing the two prompts asks whether that warning changes which underlying answer the judge selects.

Prompt condition What the judge receives Role in this study
Original The position-bias warning is retained Published prompt condition
Warning ablation Only the warning sentence is removed Demonstration manipulation

This is a demonstration manipulation rather than a novel extension. Zheng et al. had already tested a shorter prompt that removed the warning along with several other instructions.

The complete schedule contains:

12 questions × 3 answer pairs × 2 orders
× 2 prompt conditions × 3 repetitions = 432 judgments

Each judgment is sent as a new request, and the trial order is randomized. The two versions of a pair can therefore appear anywhere in the sequence rather than being administered as a fixed pair of consecutive trials.

The materials were checked before data collection

The 12 questions were chosen before Qwen was run as the judge. The audit then confirmed that each question had the required archived responses from Vicuna, Alpaca, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4, and that the prompt for comparing those responses was complete. Only after these checks were finished were the pairs sent to Qwen. This order prevents the questions from being chosen because they produced a preferred result.

Each MT-Bench question in this demonstration contains an initial question and a follow-up. The audit confirmed that every selected model answer responded to both parts. It also confirmed that writing, reasoning, STEM, and humanities were equally represented.

At the end of each judgment, Qwen reports its choice using a verdict marker. [[A]] means that the first answer was selected, while [[B]] means that the second answer was selected. The original MT-Bench format also defines [[C]] as a tie, although the forced-choice prompt used here asks Qwen to choose only A or B.

The parser looks for these markers in Qwen’s response. Because a judge may quote part of a candidate answer while explaining its decision, the audit checked that none of the candidate answers already contained the same strings. Otherwise, quoted text could be mistaken for the final verdict. All of the prompts also fit within the configured context window.

Build the schedule before sending any requests

The demonstration code and material instructions are in llm-behavior-demos. Retrieve the pinned FastChat files and four answer files, then place them in one input folder. Building the schedule does not call a model.

Why are the answers not included in the repository? The original model answers are hosted separately from the Apache-licensed FastChat code, and their page does not provide clear permission to redistribute them. The setup therefore downloads them from their original host. Their SHA-256 digests—a digital fingerprint for each file—are checked to make sure the intended files were retrieved. The details are preserved in the material audit.

From the llm-behavior-demos folder, run:

python -m position_bias_demo.build_schedule \
  --input-dir INPUT \
  --output-dir OUTPUT \
  --seed 20260815

Replace INPUT with the source-material folder and OUTPUT with the location for the new schedule. The builder verifies the SHA-256 digest of every source file and stops if a file has changed, a selected record is missing, or the prompt cannot be modified as specified.

The output contains the trial schedule and a manifest recording the source checksums, randomization seed, trial count, and schedule checksum. These files can be inspected before any model calls are made.

Run a small pilot before the complete schedule

A two-question pilot tests the procedure with 24 calls before the complete schedule is run:

python -m position_bias_demo.build_schedule \
  --input-dir INPUT \
  --output-dir PILOT_SCHEDULE \
  --seed 20260815 \
  --question-ids 81 82 \
  --comparison-files alpaca-13b.jsonl

This produces 24 trials. Run them through the model route prepared earlier in the series:

python -m position_bias_demo.run_trials \
  --schedule PILOT_SCHEDULE/trials.jsonl \
  --build-manifest PILOT_SCHEDULE/build-manifest.json \
  --run-dir PILOT_RUN \
  --model vllm-local \
  --temperature 0

The model name must match an entry in model-registry.yaml. A direct hosted API, Ollama, or Azure can be used by substituting the corresponding registry name. The resulting model environment will differ from the one used for the Qwen result reported below.

Each completed trial is saved immediately. If the run is interrupted, the collector checks the existing records and continues with the next unfinished trial. Progress can be viewed without displaying prompts or responses:

python -m position_bias_demo.track_run \
  --run-dir PILOT_RUN \
  --verify

Once the pilot has been checked, the same collection command can be used with OUTPUT/trials.jsonl and a new run directory to collect the full schedule.

The parser does not infer a verdict from the explanation

The judge explains its decision and ends the response with [[A]] or [[B]]. The complete response is saved before this verdict is extracted.

The primary rule accepts exactly one case-sensitive [[A]] or [[B]]. A missing verdict, a tie, or more than one verdict is marked invalid. The analysis does not infer a choice from the explanation or ask the model again.

The analysis is also repeated with FastChat’s original parsing rule. This is a sensitivity analysis: it checks whether using a different reasonable scoring decision changes the result. The implementation difference is documented in the material audit.

Run the analysis with:

python -m position_bias_demo.analyze \
  --schedule OUTPUT/trials.jsonl \
  --run-dir FULL_RUN \
  --output-dir ANALYSIS

How the result terms are used

Two different things can remain the “same,” so the results use more specific language:

  • A/B positional option refers to the visible position. A is the first answer shown and B is the second.
  • Underlying answer content (X/Y) refers to the actual archived model response, regardless of whether it appears in positional option A or B.
  • Same A/B positional option across repetitions means that Qwen repeated its choice when the entire prompt, including answer order, was unchanged. The content and position are both the same in this comparison.
  • Answer-identity consistency after a swap means that Qwen continued to prefer the same underlying answer content—X or Y—after it moved from A to B, or from B to A.
  • Positional-option consistency after a swap means that Qwen continued to choose A or continued to choose B after X and Y exchanged positions. The displayed position stayed the same, but the underlying answer identity changed. Across pairs, this pattern reveals a positional preference.

The repetition result concerns the first comparison. The answer-order result concerns the second.

What happened in the completed Qwen run

The completed demonstration used Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, served locally with vLLM 0.22.1. Temperature was set to 0, and the maximum response length was 1,024 tokens. All 432 scheduled judgments were collected, and every response contained a valid verdict under the primary parser.

Were identical trials repeatable?

Yes, in most cases. The 36 answer pairs were each shown in two orders, creating 72 distinct comparison prompts. Each exact prompt was sent to Qwen three times. The answer order remained fixed across these repetitions. Selecting the same option therefore meant choosing the same content in the same position; this measure cannot separate the two. It only shows whether Qwen repeated its choice when nothing in the prompt changed.

With the original judge instructions, Qwen selected the same A/B positional option on all three repetitions for 66 of the 72 prompts. For the remaining six, it selected one option twice and the other once. This produced a repetition-stability score of 97.2%.

Did swapping the answers change the judgment?

Swapping the answers changed Qwen’s preferred answer identity for 12 of the 36 pairs. In these cases, Qwen kept choosing the same A/B positional option after X and Y exchanged positions. Six pairs consistently favored A, the first position, and six consistently favored B, the second position.

For the remaining 24 pairs, Qwen continued to prefer the same underlying answer content, X or Y, after it moved to the other position. These were answer-identity-consistent choices.

The result was therefore not driven by a single overall preference for the first or the second position.

Did removing the warning make a clear difference?

No clear difference appeared in this small sample. After the warning was removed, Qwen preferred the same underlying answer content across positions for 25 of the 36 pairs, compared with 24 under the original prompt. The number of pairs in which it switched to the other content fell from 12 to 11. Identical repetitions also remained similar: the same A/B positional option was selected on all three repetitions for 67 of 72 prompts, compared with 66 of 72 before the warning was removed.

A one-pair difference is not enough to conclude that removing the warning increased or reduced position bias. Repeating the analysis with FastChat’s original parser produced the same result.

How this result relates to the published study

Shi et al. found that all 15 judges sometimes changed their choice after the answers were swapped. Depending on the judge, the same underlying answer was retained in 57% to 82% of comparisons (Shi et al., 2025). Qwen retained the same underlying answer for 24 of 36 pairs, or 66.7%, in this demonstration. These percentages are not directly comparable because the models, questions, answers, and generation settings differ.

The design, source record, model responses, analysis tables, and parser checks are available in llm-behavior-demos.
